title: The response of marine mussels to low dissolved inorganic carbon and high pH conditions under direct ocean carbon capture and storage (DOCCS)
content:
Abstract
Direct Ocean Carbon Capture and Storage (DOCCS) is a novel marine Carbon Dioxide Removal (mCDR) technique that facilitates atmospheric carbon removal by extracting dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) from seawater. Low DIC seawater, which due to low carbonic acid concentrations has a high pH, is released into the marine environment where it takes up atmospheric CO2. Potential unintended environmental impacts are considered a challenge for the development and scaling of DOCCS as little is known about the response of marine ecosystems to low-DIC, high-pH seawater. This study investigates the short-term physiological response and recovery of intertidal mussels, Mytilus spp., to three concentrations of low-DIC, high-pH seawater (80%, 60%, and 40% decarbonized, respectively) and a control of unmanipulated seawater. Mussel mortality, oxygen consumption, and ammonium excretion were measured after a 48-h exposure to the decarbonized water and a 48-h recovery period. While low-DIC, high-pH seawater did not cause significant mortality (1.3% in the 80% and 60% treatments, zero in all others), we observed spawning and reduced oxygen consumption indicative of an avoidance response (i.e. extended periods of valve closure) in the 80% and 60% treatments. Mineral precipitation was observed in the 60% and 80% treatments and may have contributed to observed mussel responses. When ambient seawater conditions were restored, mussel oxygen consumption and ammonium excretion increased towards and sometimes above control values, suggesting the capacity for recovery. These results show how natural mussel populations could be impacted in a scenario of large-scale DOCCS deployment, where the amount of decarbonized water is high and/or the proximity to the discharge point is high, i.e. level of dilution is low.
